prompt: A ray meets a flat glass surface. From which line is the angle of incidence measured in Snell's law?
options: The horizontal
The surface itself
The reflected ray
The normal to the surface
explanation: Snell's law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, defines both angles from the normal. Measuring from the surface gives the complementary angle and a wrong answer.
hint: Recall which line the angles are drawn from in a ray diagram.

prompt: A plane mirror forms a virtual image. Why can you not catch it on a screen placed at the image position?
answer: No actual light rays arrive there, since they only appear to diverge from it
options: No actual light rays arrive there, since they only appear to diverge from it
The mirror absorbs the light that forms the image
A screen blocks the rays before they converge
The image is too dim to be projected
explanation: A virtual image is where the diverging rays appear to come from. A real image needs rays to converge there so that a screen can intercept the light.
hint: Ask whether light actually passes through the image point.

prompt: You enlarge a blurry telescope image of two close stars further. Will they separate?
answer: Not necessarily: diffraction limits the detail regardless of magnification
options: Not necessarily: diffraction limits the detail regardless of magnification
Yes, because more magnification always adds detail, so enlarging the image separates the two stars
Yes, but only above a certain magnification
No, because magnification removes the second star
explanation: Magnification scales the existing pattern. The detail is limited by aperture diffraction and aberrations, so past a point you just get a larger blur.
hint: Magnifying a low-resolution photo shows the same pixels, only larger.

A thin converging lens has f=15 cm and a real object at u=30 cm. With 1/f=1/u+1/v, find v in cm.
A real object sits exactly one focal length from a thin converging lens. What does the paraxial model predict?
answer: The refracted rays emerge parallel, so no finite image forms
options: A virtual image forms at the same point as the object, since the rays from the focal point diverge
A real image forms at twice the focal length
The lens forms an image of the same size
The refracted rays emerge parallel, so no finite image forms
explanation: From 1/u + 1/v = 1/f with u = f, 1/v = 0, so v → ∞. Rays from a point on the focus leave the lens parallel to each other.
hint: Put u = f into the lens equation and see what happens to 1/v.

For those distances, find signed transverse magnification.
A single thin-lens calculation predicts a sharp point image. Why might a real lens still give a blurry spot?
answer: The thin-lens model assumes paraxial rays, ignoring aberrations
options: Real lenses have no focal length, so the thin-lens equation fails
Light does not obey Snell's law at the edge
The equation includes the aberrations, but they are small
The thin-lens model assumes paraxial rays, ignoring aberrations
hint: Recall the conditions under which the thin-lens formula is derived.
explanation: The thin-lens equation is a paraxial approximation for rays near the axis at small angles. Spherical aberration and similar effects appear when the aperture is large.

explanation: 1/v=0.1-0.2=-0.1 per cm, so v=-10 cm. The negative coordinate puts the upright virtual image on the object side; it does not indicate a negative physical separation.
